newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault orders study on Belgian closure options.
newsitem.headline: Renault orders study on Belgian closure options.

text.p: French carmaker Renault said on Tuesday it had commissioned an independent study to explore alternatives to the proposed closure of the Vilvoorde assembly plant that sparked an outcry in France and Belgium.

The decision, coming less than two weeks after the French Socialists' election victory, appeared to be a response to pressure from the new government which controls the state's 46 percent stake in the loss-making privatised firm.

After refusing for months to budge on the decision announced in February, Renault Chairman Louis Schweitzer told the annual general meeting that the board had approved an independent study and would meet again before the end of June to assess its results.
The compromise angered union leaders who said it held out false hope to the 2,900 workers still employed at the plant since a thorough study could not be conducted in three weeks.

The move also worried investors, who drove the share down nearly five percent on concerns that the new government might block or delay a much-needed restructuring of Renault, which lost 5.25 billion francs ($909.3 million) last year.
Government officials said the decision represented the kind of conciliatory behaviour they hope to encourage.
"We can no longer accept these abrupt decisions to close sites," said an aide to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
"Prime Minister Jospin made commitments during his campaign ... and it seemed essential to use Vilvoorde as an illustration that he would do what he said he would," he told reporters.
The independent study was confided to Danielle Kaisergruber of Bernard Bruhnes consultancy, a Renault statement said.
Tensions ran high at Renault's annual meeting, which was disrupted by Belgian workers shouting "Schweitzer go" and "Vilvoorde, Vilvoorde" during the chairman's presentation.

The closure, scheduled for July 31, provoked a storm of political and union protest when it was announced. The factory is in the hometown of Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who met Jospin in Paris last Saturday to appeal for a review.

Renault has argued that the plant closure is part of an essential reorganisation of its European car assembly operations, which are far more scattered and costly than those of its bigger rivals in the European industry.
Its annual production per site averages 125,000 cars compared with more than 200,000 at Ford, GM Opel and Volkswagen.
Company officials say union proposals for shorter working hours and job-sharing would not achieve the same purpose.
"After the Vilvoorde closure, our industrial operations would be well positioned from here to the year 2000," Schweitzer said.

"In the event that the study leads the company to confirm its initial decision, a plan would be immediately implemented, including on the one hand the appropriate social measures and, on the other hand, the establishment of a significant industrial activity on the site," the Renault statement said.
Renault-Vilvoorde workers, who staged a long occupation of the plant after the closure was announced, began another three-day strike on Monday.
The Renault statement said the board renewed its confidence in Schweitzer. But analysts wondered whether he would be allowed to make the decisions that he believed were necessary.
"It's highly unclear who is running this company," said a London-based analyst, "Renault have been passing themselves off as independent... As an investor, I'd feel safer on the sidelines."
The stock ended down 4.63 percent at 127.80 francs ($21.96).
Analysts in Paris were more confident that the new government would concede, after examining the situation, that tough measures were essential for Renault.
"The Socialists don't want to ruffle anybody," said a Paris broker. "They want an independent expert to make the decision in order to make it more palatable."
